OK — I've gone through all three attachments (TIKR market data + multiples history, Q1 2026 earnings call, Q3 2025 earnings call), both Excel files (LSEG financials and analyst recommendations), and your ITRI thesis. Here's the honest read.

**They are two completely distinct businesses.** The only surface connection is the word "edge."

**Advantech** makes industrial PCs, embedded boards, and edge computing hardware. Their customers are OEMs across dozens of verticals — semiconductor equipment builders, medical device companies, transportation operators, factory automation integrators. They are a platform hardware company. When they say "Edge AI," they mean bolting GPU acceleration onto their existing IPC product line so factory robots and MRI machines can run inference locally. Edge AI was 20.5% of Q1 2026 revenue (USD 132M), and 93% of that was product hardware — only 6.8% was pure component buy-and-sell. The CEO was explicit: "most revenue is still generated from our edge computing and devices."

**Itron** sells smart meters and a recurring-revenue software platform to water, gas, and electric utilities. When they say "Grid Edge Intelligence," they mean a SaaS layer running on 17.5M deployed endpoints that utilities pay annually to monitor and manage their networks. The business you're invested in is the ARR ramp — $368M growing 20%+ YoY at 39–76% margins, buried inside a hardware multiple.

These companies don't compete, don't share customers, don't share technology stacks, and aren't substitutes for each other in any portfolio construction sense. Different industry buckets entirely.

**Now the valuation — this is where it gets important for your framework.**

Advantech at NT$719 is trading at:
- 32.4x NTM P/E (up from 23x in Dec 2025)
- 24.8x NTM EV/EBITDA
- 46x LTM P/E
- 40x LTM EV/EBITDA

The stock has done **127% in one year** from a NT$271 52-week low. It's NT$35 off the 52-week high of NT$754.

Consensus from the LSEG data: 5 Strong Buy, 10 Buy, 2 Hold, 0 Sell. Mean target NT$749.50 — that's **4.2% above the current price**. The stock has essentially run to consensus. Yuanta has the highest target at NT$870 and even that's only 21% upside.

The forward growth numbers are real — fwd 2-yr revenue CAGR 31.4%, EPS CAGR 39%, the B/B ratio hit 1.77 in Q1 with 47% of bookings scheduled for 6+ month delivery. Semiconductor equipment, factory automation, and the DDR4/DDR5 supply crunch are all pulling orders forward. Management has pricing power (bi-weekly ASP adjustments on systems, monthly on boards). The business quality is legitimate — 26% ROE, 24% ROIC, net cash balance sheet, 39% gross margins.

**But here's the problem through your lens:**

There is no measurement-lag arbitrage here. Run it against your own checklist:

**Consensus delta?** None. 15 out of 17 analysts say buy. The Edge AI transition is the consensus narrative, not an undiscovered one. Every sell-side note already models the 30% Edge AI contribution target.

**Structural blind spot?** No. Unlike ITRI where zero analysts had built a standalone software SOTP, Advantech's Edge AI contribution is disclosed quarterly, tracked by every covering analyst, and the company literally presents it in every earnings call. The information is priced.

**Forcing function?** No dated catalyst that mechanically forces consensus to update. COMPUTEX presentations are already previewed. There's no "Investor Day" moment where a hidden business segment gets revealed.

**Misclassified asset?** No. Advantech is a premium industrial hardware compounder and the market is pricing it as exactly that. ITRI is a software business hiding in a hardware wrapper — that's the dislocation. Advantech's Edge AI revenue is hardware with AI chips attached. There's no buried recurring revenue stream trading at the wrong multiple.

The stock went from NT$271 to NT$719 because the market figured out the Edge AI cycle. That repricing already happened. You'd be buying after the 127% move, paying 32x forward earnings, with the street target 4% away.

This is a well-run business at a full price. It's the opposite of your ITRI setup.

## **4.3 What Convertible Arb Funds Are Doing**

Convertible arbitrage funds buy the note and simultaneously short the stock to delta-hedge. They are not making a fundamental bet against Itron — they are extracting implied volatility embedded in the conversion option. The short is a mathematical hedge, not a view on the business.

That is implicit agreement that the stock reaches +40% above current price. The arb short covers mechanically on conversion. The concurrent buyback (1,050,309 shares) further reduced available float on the same day the arb shorts were established. |

The Investor Day creates simultaneous demand into structurally thin supply. Three mechanisms activate independently on the same event.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Short Squeeze | 4,967,939 shares (5.5× DTC) | Investor Day SOTP publication | Fundamental shorts have no model to hide behind. Arb shorts cover at $123.77. Both buy into ~650K ADV. |
| 2. Fund Initiation | 439K shares = 49% of ADV per 1% built | Two consecutive ARR prints ≥18% (Apr 30 is gate 1) | Growth funds begin initiating simultaneously. Each 1% position takes multiple days to build before price moves against the buyer. |
| 3. Dealer Delta Hedge | $700M notional, $123.77→$190.42 range | Stock rises toward conversion price | Banks sold capped calls to Itron and are short gamma. As stock rises they must buy shares to hedge. Programmed mechanical buying. |

All three mechanisms are independent. None requires the other to function. All three activate on the same event.

OK — I've gone through all three attachments (TIKR market data + multiples history, Q1 2026 earnings call, Q3 2025 earnings call), both Excel files (LSEG financials and analyst recommendations), and your ITRI thesis. Here's the honest read.

**They are two completely distinct businesses.** The only surface connection is the word "edge."

**Advantech** makes industrial PCs, embedded boards, and edge computing hardware. Their customers are OEMs across dozens of verticals — semiconductor equipment builders, medical device companies, transportation operators, factory automation integrators. They are a platform hardware company. When they say "Edge AI," they mean bolting GPU acceleration onto their existing IPC product line so factory robots and MRI machines can run inference locally. Edge AI was 20.5% of Q1 2026 revenue (USD 132M), and 93% of that was product hardware — only 6.8% was pure component buy-and-sell. The CEO was explicit: "most revenue is still generated from our edge computing and devices."

**Itron** sells smart meters and a recurring-revenue software platform to water, gas, and electric utilities. When they say "Grid Edge Intelligence," they mean a SaaS layer running on 17.5M deployed endpoints that utilities pay annually to monitor and manage their networks. The business you're invested in is the ARR ramp — $368M growing 20%+ YoY at 39–76% margins, buried inside a hardware multiple.

These companies don't compete, don't share customers, don't share technology stacks, and aren't substitutes for each other in any portfolio construction sense. Different industry buckets entirely.

**Now the valuation — this is where it gets important for your framework.**

Advantech at NT$719 is trading at:
- 32.4x NTM P/E (up from 23x in Dec 2025)
- 24.8x NTM EV/EBITDA
- 46x LTM P/E
- 40x LTM EV/EBITDA

The stock has done **127% in one year** from a NT$271 52-week low. It's NT$35 off the 52-week high of NT$754.

Consensus from the LSEG data: 5 Strong Buy, 10 Buy, 2 Hold, 0 Sell. Mean target NT$749.50 — that's **4.2% above the current price**. The stock has essentially run to consensus. Yuanta has the highest target at NT$870 and even that's only 21% upside.

The forward growth numbers are real — fwd 2-yr revenue CAGR 31.4%, EPS CAGR 39%, the B/B ratio hit 1.77 in Q1 with 47% of bookings scheduled for 6+ month delivery. Semiconductor equipment, factory automation, and the DDR4/DDR5 supply crunch are all pulling orders forward. Management has pricing power (bi-weekly ASP adjustments on systems, monthly on boards). The business quality is legitimate — 26% ROE, 24% ROIC, net cash balance sheet, 39% gross margins.

**But here's the problem through your lens:**

There is no measurement-lag arbitrage here. Run it against your own checklist:

**Consensus delta?** None. 15 out of 17 analysts say buy. The Edge AI transition is the consensus narrative, not an undiscovered one. Every sell-side note already models the 30% Edge AI contribution target.

**Structural blind spot?** No. Unlike ITRI where zero analysts had built a standalone software SOTP, Advantech's Edge AI contribution is disclosed quarterly, tracked by every covering analyst, and the company literally presents it in every earnings call. The information is priced.

**Forcing function?** No dated catalyst that mechanically forces consensus to update. COMPUTEX presentations are already previewed. There's no "Investor Day" moment where a hidden business segment gets revealed.

**Misclassified asset?** No. Advantech is a premium industrial hardware compounder and the market is pricing it as exactly that. ITRI is a software business hiding in a hardware wrapper — that's the dislocation. Advantech's Edge AI revenue is hardware with AI chips attached. There's no buried recurring revenue stream trading at the wrong multiple.

The stock went from NT$271 to NT$719 because the market figured out the Edge AI cycle. That repricing already happened. You'd be buying after the 127% move, paying 32x forward earnings, with the street target 4% away.

This is a well-run business at a full price. It's the opposite of your ITRI setup.

chat_messages.text:
Good question, and honestly the answer is kind of infuriating from your ITRI thesis perspective.

Advantech doesn't "deserve" 32x forward earnings on fundamentals alone. What it has is **narrative clarity** — and that's doing all the heavy lifting on the multiple.

**The market pays for labels, not substance.** Advantech slapped "Edge AI" on its industrial PCs, disclosed it as a revenue line (20.5% of Q1, growing 67% YoY), and gave every analyst a clean story to write: "Edge AI platform company riding the inference-at-the-edge wave." Seventeen analysts are all telling the same story. The B/B ratio at 1.77 (US at 2.37) gives visible, confirmable growth — you can literally see the revenue coming six months out because 47% of Q1 bookings have delivery dates past that horizon. The market loves certainty, and Advantech is handing it on a platter.

Now compare that to Itron. You have $368M in ARR growing 20%+ with 39-76% margins — that's a *real* software business inside a hardware wrapper. But the market can't see it because:

- Management doesn't break out ARR as a headline metric the way a SaaS company would. You have to dig into the 10-K to find it.
- Nine analysts cover it and literally zero do a standalone software SOTP. They all model it as one blended industrial business.
- The company is classified as "metering infrastructure" — it sits in the utilities/industrials bucket, not the software or AI bucket.

So the irony is this: **Advantech is getting a software-like multiple for selling hardware with an AI chip on it, while Itron is getting a hardware multiple despite having an actual recurring software business.** The market is paying 32x NTM P/E for Advantech's *narrative* of software-adjacent growth, while burying Itron's *actual* software at ~8.8x EV/ARR inside a blended hardware multiple.

That's not Advantech being overvalued or Itron being undervalued in some abstract sense — it's the measurement lag you're betting on. The market's classification system is the bottleneck. Advantech made it easy for the sell-side to re-rate it: one clean revenue disclosure ("Edge AI is X% of revenue") and a catchy theme. Itron hasn't done that yet for its software layer, and until something forces the reclassification — Investor Day, a segment reshuffle, an activist, an acquirer running a SOTP — the nine analysts will keep modeling it as a monolithic industrial and the multiple stays compressed.

The Advantech comp actually sharpens your thesis. It proves the market *will* pay a premium for embedded intelligence at the edge — it just needs the story packaged right. Itron's software is a better business than Advantech's "Edge AI" by every margin metric, but it's invisible to the pricing mechanism. That's your edge.

How MarketFighter built a 3,600+ subscriber Substack about investing, reached 100+ paid subscribers in under five months, and quit his job to live off his investment strategy.


This is an interview with MarketFighter of The MarketFighter Strategy.

At a glance:
Current subscriber count: 3,600

Most successful post: My Investment Approach that Outperformed the Stock Market in 25 of 26 Years

Most underrated growth tactic: Posting notes every day.

Favorite Substack feature: The detailed growth statistics where I can see where new subscribers came from.

One creator everyone should follow: The Private Ledger. He’s a great writer covering companies before they go public.

One tool you can’t live without: My Excel sheets (old-school, I know).

Key metric to track: Subscriber count, both free and paid.

Main revenue source: Paid subscriptions (aside from investing).

One sentence describing your newsletter: I share my simple ETF investment strategy with investors who value consistency and rational decisions.

One piece of advice for new writers: Spend more time on Notes than you expect!

The Beginning
Tell us a bit about yourself to begin with.
I’m a software engineer and investor living in Denmark. I’m 41, living with my wife and our two sons. I consider myself a family man and prioritize it highly. Investing has been a passion of mine for many years, with the goal to achieve financial freedom. Earlier this year I quit my software developer job to live off my investment strategy.

Tell us about your publication. What do you write about and who is it for?
I write about stock market investing from a strategic and evidence-based perspective (no business analysis). I don’t go deep into academic theory, but I present useful findings from research.

Most importantly, I share my own monthly ETF strategy. It’s a rules-based approach I developed five years ago based on a combination of research findings, and I’ve had great results with this strategy.

I write for anyone who cares about optimizing investment returns and has the discipline to follow a systematic approach. I share the exact trades and the full strategy with paid subscribers.

What was your investment and writing journey before Substack?
I started investing in 2004 when I was 18 and inherited an amount roughly equal to $10,000 today. I honestly had no idea what I was doing back then. But it somehow ignited a passion for investing, and I spent the better part of two decades hunting for high-probability ways to optimize returns.

In early 2021 it felt like the stars aligned, as I managed to build a relatively simple system based on all my research findings. Backtesting revealed significant and very consistent market outperformance over the previous 20 years.

I still remember the exact moment on one particular night, when I realized I had discovered something out of the ordinary.

Since then I have invested the majority of my money following this approach. In April 2026 I quit my job as a software engineer, as my returns from investing in the system kept growing.

You spent years developing your investment strategy before launching the publication. What made you decide to start sharing it publicly?
To be honest, in the beginning I was skeptical. What I had found seemed a bit too good to be true based on everything I knew about how markets work. I just waited for it to somehow stop working.

But it didn’t stop, and the pattern I had seen in my backtests continued as I traded it with real money on the table.

After around five years I felt much more confident in the long-term value of my strategy. In the meantime I had gotten increasingly tired of my day job, and I dreamt of an independent life centered around my passion for investing.

That’s where Substack came into the picture. I had never published any writing before, but I figured it could be the perfect match for me.

What made Substack the right platform for this particular business?
Three things were in play here:

1. After five years of great results with my system, I felt it was time to share the strategy and my performance publicly.

2. While I considered quitting my job, I also knew I would need one or more new projects to wake up to every morning in a new independent life.

3. Investment returns tend to go up and down a lot. I was hoping to find a way to add a more consistent side-income to my returns.

I soon found out that Substack could be the solution that ticked all the boxes.

The Growth Story
What did your first few months on Substack look like?
I started on March 1st this year. I knew from other stories that the beginning tends to be slow, so I had no expectations. After 22 days I had my first 100 subscribers. This surprised me, and it gave me a feeling that this project had real potential.

After six or seven weeks, subscribers started reaching out to ask me why I didn’t charge money for my service. One of them even said he hoped I would do it soon, so that he could count on me not to suddenly stop delivering. That’s when I knew people really found value in my work.

You’re now at around 3,500 subscribers and #19 Rising in Finance. Can you walk us through how you got there?
It has been a fairly steady journey so far. While growth in the early months was already faster than I expected, it has been slightly accelerating since then. On most days I get 20-30 new subscribers now.

I had no initial network or following on other platforms, so it’s just organic growth on Substack, starting from 0.

I did a single post on Reddit, but I found that engaging directly with the Substack community gave much more meaningful interaction. Posting notes every day has definitely been a key driver.

What did your growth look like at key milestones like 100, 500, 1,000, and 2,000 subscribers?
In general there has been a compounding effect, and my growth seems to increase over time, at least so far. My first 100 subscribers took longer (22 days) than my last 400 for instance. From time to time, I’ve had a few days where it slowed down, but not for months.

For me, my biggest milestone so far was not a subscriber count, but receiving the Substack Bestseller badge in July, as I reached more than 100 paid subscribers. I’ve been absolutely blown away by the early support and the fact that this already happened less than five months in.

What’s one thing that worked much better than you expected?
The community.

Do you actively use Notes? If so, what kinds of Notes bring you the most subscribers?
Every single day.

In general most subscribers find me through notes where I clearly express what it is I’m doing (giving them a good idea of why they should consider subscribing).

Also, notes with a personal touch that readers can relate to or milestone celebrations tend to bring a good number of new subscribers.

Trust & Investing Content
Building an audience around investing requires a lot of trust. How did you establish credibility?
It’s a good question. I try to be myself and be honest in everything I do. I publish open performance metrics every month, and anyone can go back and look them up if they want to. I don’t try to hide bad numbers. Many subscribers have reached out to tell me that this transparency means a lot.

Another factor might be that I have a long story behind what I’m doing. I’ve been investing for 22 years, done an extensive amount of research, and I’ve personally traded the same strategy with my own money for more than five years now.

How do you decide which parts of your strategy to explain for free and which belong behind the paid subscription?
I decided from the beginning to only put my trading signals behind the paywall. These are needed for people who want to follow my strategy. I wanted everything else to be publicly available, so more people can find it and engage around it.

How much of your content comes from your investment research versus ideas from conversations with readers?
Most of my content comes from research, but the decisions on what to focus on in my articles are definitely inspired by comments and messages from readers.

I love the ongoing feedback I get, as it helps me judge what readers are missing and what they want to know more about.

How often do you publish, and how did you arrive at that publishing rhythm?
I have two fixed monthly articles: My trading signal, and my monthly performance report. Aside from these, I publish anything between 1 and 4 articles with strategic market insights.

I did not settle on a fixed publishing scheme, like publishing once every week. I prefer to publish the right thing when it’s ready, and not because I set a deadline.

What metrics do you actually pay attention to?
The subscriber counts are the most important to me, both the free subscribers and the paid.

I rarely check my follower count.

Open rates are interesting as well.

Do you think the high-stakes nature of investing makes readers more cautious about subscribing or paying?
Actually, I think it’s the other way around. When readers can see a tangible monetary benefit from subscribing, they can quickly decide if it’s worth it for their case or not.

Every time I get 17 new subscribers, one of them ends up upgrading to the paid tier, according to my statistics. I’m very satisfied with that.

The Business Side
What does your monetization model look like today?
It’s paid subscriptions and nothing else. I have a monthly plan at $45, and a yearly one at $375 (30% off versus the monthly plan).

What kind of free content converts readers into paid subscribers most effectively?
It has very much been the articles where I explain my strategy, show how it has performed, and the small notes about how it has affected my own life.

What’s your goal for the next 12 months?
I rarely set specific numbers for goals, but I do everything I can to continue growing and learning, as more and more people find my Substack.

Every single new subscriber means a lot to me, and my plan is to continue doing this for many years to come.

What are you currently experimenting with on Substack?
Collaborating with other writers. I have started writing articles together with six other finance writers to share our different perspectives on investing. This interview is also a new step for me.

If someone had 100 subscribers today, what would you tell them to focus on for the next 30 days?
I would focus on notes and post at least one every day. Of course the substance of the articles means a lot as well, but it’s the notes that get people’s attention.

Where do you think Substack is heading as a platform, and what opportunities do you see opening up for creators?
There has been a lot of discussion around this lately. I think it will keep growing, and competition will increase. For creators, my guess is:

If you’re just providing content that looks like everyone else’s, it will be tough. But if you have a unique offering that readers won’t find elsewhere, you will thrive.

That’s my two cents.

Your style is working — and the engagement pattern is the proof. When someone like No Shooting Blanks (who writes like they've actually run money) comes back three times on the same thread pushing you to decompose the China discount further, that's not a 70-subscriber interaction. That's the kind of back-and-forth that happens on research desks. The Arbor Letter engaging on management guidance accuracy, QSG Quant Research pushing back on survivorship bias — these are people with real analytical frameworks responding to yours because you're giving them something to work with.

The reason larger accounts are engaging is the same reason your notes outperform the feed: you're posting primary source work, not takes. A note citing Bradshaw, Brown, and Huang with the actual hit rate and forecast error numbers is something a 5,000-subscriber account would write. Most people at your sub count are posting "what's your favorite stock?" and getting one-word ticker replies. You're getting multi-reply threads because the notes have enough substance to disagree with.

That said — your writing style in notes is slightly different from your posts, and that's actually fine. The posts are more structured, first-person, data-derived, the whole profile. The notes are looser, more conversational, more question-driven. That's the right split. Don't try to make every note sound like a post. The notes are the top of funnel, the posts are where the work lives.

**Next notes to post** — a few that play to what's already working:

"The market is paying 32x forward earnings for a Taiwanese hardware company that put 'Edge AI' in its revenue breakdown. A US mid-cap with $368M in actual recurring software revenue at 20%+ growth trades at a lower multiple. The label matters more than the business underneath it."

That's the Advantech/Itron insight from tonight distilled into a note. It's specific, it has a tension, and it invites people to argue about whether the label premium is justified or lazy. Don't name the companies in the note — let people ask.

"Sell-side target prices are met 38% of the time. Management guidance is met closer to 70-80% depending on the study. The market ignores both of them selectively. Trying to figure out when and why."

That's a follow-up to the Bradshaw note and the Arbor Letter thread. It signals you're doing the work and it invites people who have an opinion on guidance accuracy to weigh in.

"Name a company where the market's classification of what the business is doesn't match what the business actually does. Not the stock being cheap — the business being misunderstood at a category level."

That's your measurement-lag thesis turned into a community question. It's the kind of note that gets 15+ replies because everyone has an example, and some of those examples might actually be worth researching.

"What's the most useful thing you've pulled from a 10-K that wasn't in the earnings call or any sell-side note?"

Primary source discipline as a conversation starter. Directly on brand and it filters for the kind of readers you actually want.

The pattern with your best notes: they either show a specific piece of work you did (the sell-side accuracy data, the NetEase/Meta matched-margin screen) or they ask a question that can only be answered well by someone who's done real work (how do you set price targets, what's the market overlooking). Keep alternating between those two types.

Paul Bohlen
SpaceX Is Really a Cost-Curve Company
SpaceX isn’t just making rockets cheaper—it’s making an entire orbital economy economically possible.
Paul Bohlen
Sep 30, 2026
SpaceX is often described as a rocket company, a satellite company, or an internet company.

Those descriptions miss the deeper thesis.

SpaceX is fundamentally a cost-curve company.

Its strategy is to repeatedly reduce the cost of accessing and operating in space, then use those lower costs to make entirely new markets economically viable.

The rocket is the starting point—not the end market.

1. Start with the launch cost curve

The first constraint is simple: getting hardware into orbit is expensive.

SpaceX attacked that constraint through reusable rockets, higher launch cadence, and increasingly standardized operations.

The important effect isn’t simply that each launch becomes cheaper. Lower launch costs change the economics of everything that comes afterward.

When it becomes cheaper to put another satellite into orbit, companies can deploy more capacity. More capacity creates more services and expands the potential market for space-based infrastructure.

The key isn’t simply cheaper launches.

It’s what cheaper access to space makes possible.

2. Reuse changes the economics

Traditional rockets treated much of the vehicle as expendable.

SpaceX increasingly treats the rocket as infrastructure that can be reused.

That changes the economics from:

Build → launch → discard

to:

Build → launch → recover → relaunch.

The more frequently hardware can be reused, the more launches can be supported by the same underlying capital base.

That matters because utilization is a major component of infrastructure economics.

A rocket sitting on the ground generates little economic value.

A rocket flying repeatedly can generate value across many missions.

3. Lower costs expand the market

Cheaper launch doesn’t just make existing space businesses more profitable.

It expands the set of things that are economically possible.

If launching one satellite costs too much, a company may deploy ten.

If launch costs fall dramatically, deploying hundreds or thousands becomes conceivable.

The question changes from:

“Can we afford to launch this?”

to:

“What can we build if launching it is cheap?”

This is where the cost curve becomes more important than the rocket itself.

4. Utilization creates an operational advantage

More launches also create more operational experience.

Higher cadence can improve turnaround time, reliability, manufacturing efficiency, logistics, maintenance, and supply chains.

That creates an advantage that isn’t purely technological.

A competitor can build a reusable rocket.

It is much harder to immediately replicate the infrastructure and operational experience required to fly that rocket repeatedly at high utilization.

The competitive advantage therefore becomes the system, not just the vehicle.

5. Scale changes the economics of infrastructure

Once launch becomes cheaper, the next opportunity is deploying more infrastructure.

More satellites can support larger networks.

Larger networks can support more users.

More users can generate more revenue.

Starlink illustrates the broader concept: lower launch costs make it possible to deploy and replenish a massive satellite network that would have been far more difficult under older launch economics.

At sufficient scale, the economics begin to resemble infrastructure rather than traditional aerospace.

And infrastructure becomes more valuable as utilization rises.

6. The second-order economy

This is where the thesis gets much larger.

If access to orbit becomes inexpensive enough, entirely new categories can become economically interesting:

Orbital manufacturing

Space-based computing

Solar energy collection

Large-scale communications infrastructure

In-space servicing

Defense infrastructure

Eventually, industrial activity beyond Earth

These markets don’t need to exist today for the cost curve to matter.

They only need to become possible as the cost of accessing space falls.

The same pattern has appeared throughout industrial history:

Lower cost → greater adoption → greater scale → new applications.

Space may be entering that phase.

7. The infrastructure moat

The ultimate advantage may therefore not be any single SpaceX product.

It may be the infrastructure underneath all of them.

Lower launch costs enable more satellites.

More satellites create more connectivity.

More infrastructure creates more potential demand for launches.

And higher utilization can push the cost of the entire system lower.

That is more powerful than a rocket company.

It is a cost-reduction engine for an emerging economy.

But there is a physical limit.

Orbit has finite volume. Spectrum is constrained. Power generation and thermal rejection create engineering limits. Collision risk rises with congestion. And launch capacity itself can eventually become a bottleneck.

So the long-term thesis isn’t simply about putting more things into orbit.

It is about whether the economics of building in space improve faster than the physical constraints tighten.

That leads to the question I think matters most:

At what point does the cost of reaching orbit become cheaper than the cost of building the infrastructure once you get there?

Honest thoughts on the article itself: it's a framework essay, not an analysis. The cost-curve thesis is real — Wright's Law, experience curves, the pattern where unit costs decline as cumulative production scales. You see it in semiconductors, solar panels, Model T assembly lines. Applying that lens to SpaceX is a legitimate move.

But the piece has no numbers in it. No cost-per-kg to orbit over time, no Falcon 9 reflight economics, no Starship projected unit costs, no Starlink subscriber economics, no margin structure. It describes the *shape* of the argument ("lower cost → greater adoption → greater scale → new applications") without actually measuring any of it. That's the difference between a framework and a thesis. The framework tells you what to look for. The thesis tells you what you found.

And the deeper problem: SpaceX is private. There's no 10-K, no quarterly transcript, no DEF 14A. You literally cannot do the primary-source work you'd want to do. So the article is stuck at the conceptual level by necessity, not by choice. The ending question — "at what point does the cost of reaching orbit become cheaper than the cost of building the infrastructure once you get there?" — is actually the most interesting line in the piece, but it's also the one that would require real numbers to answer, and those numbers don't exist publicly.

The second-order economy stuff (orbital manufacturing, space-based computing, solar energy collection) is speculative. The article says "these markets don't need to exist today for the cost curve to matter" — which is true, but it also means the bull case is unfalsifiable until those markets either materialize or don't.

Two likes, three restacks in 13 days. Modest engagement. Bohlen's basically using your note as a distribution channel, which is normal Substack behavior — nothing wrong with it, everyone does it.

For your reply to him:

---

The cost-curve framing is interesting. Wright's Law shows up across industries where cumulative production drives unit cost down — semiconductors, solar, batteries. Applying it to launch economics makes sense conceptually.

The part I keep coming back to is that SpaceX is private, so you can't actually verify the slope of the curve with filings. The framework tells you what to look for but without the unit economics being public, it's hard to move from "this pattern should apply" to "here's where we are on the curve and here's the implied margin structure at scale." The question you end with — when does reaching orbit get cheaper than building once you're there — is the right one. But it's also the one that needs real numbers to answer.

Appreciate you sharing the piece.

---

Short, engages with the actual content, doesn't pretend to know SpaceX's financials, and stays in your lane. You're a public-markets guy who works from filings — being honest about that limitation is more credible than faking a SpaceX opinion.
